## Overview

The solution is split into two files, the way the `Summarizer` example in the
lecture is: [`binom.hpp`](binom.hpp) holds the class and its member functions,
and [`lab-solutions.cpp`](lab-solutions.cpp) holds only `main()` and starts
with `#include "binom.hpp"`. Quotes (instead of angle brackets) tell the
compiler to look for the header next to the source file. To compile and run:

```bash
g++ -std=c++17 -Wall -o lab-solutions lab-solutions.cpp
./lab-solutions
```

Only the `.cpp` file is passed to the compiler; the header is pulled in by the
`#include`. The header is wrapped in an include guard

```cpp
#ifndef BINOM_HPP
#define BINOM_HPP
// ... contents ...
#endif
```

so that including it twice in the same translation unit does not define the
class twice. The member functions are defined `inline` for the same reason:
their definitions live in a header that may be included from several `.cpp`
files.

Keeping everything in one `.cpp` file also works and is what you would do for
a throwaway program. The split starts paying off as soon as more than one
program needs the class.

The class declaration is the one given in the lab. Notice that all four member
functions are declared `const`: they only read `n` and `p`, they never modify
the object.

```cpp
#include <cmath>
#include <cstdio>

class Binom {
private:
  int n;
  double p;

public:
  Binom(int n_, double p_) : n(n_), p(p_) {};
  int factorial(int k) const;
  double choose(int a, int b) const;
  double dbinom(int k) const;
  void print(int k) const;
};
```

The member-initializer list (`: n(n_), p(p_)`) is preferred over assigning
inside the body of the constructor: the members are initialized directly
instead of being default-constructed and then overwritten.

To see why, it helps to know that every constructor runs in two phases. First
all data members are initialized, in the order in which they are *declared* in
the class; this happens before the opening `{` of the body is reached. Only
then does the body run, with every member already holding a value. The
initializer list is our only chance to take part in the first phase -- any
member we leave out of it is initialized for us, by calling its default
constructor.

Note that `n(n_)` is not a function call. The parentheses are initialization
syntax, the same ones as in `int x(5);`. The name in front of them is looked up
among the class members, the expression inside is evaluated in the scope of the
constructor. For an `int` or a `double` no constructor is involved at all: the
value is simply copied into place. For a class-type member, the compiler picks
a constructor of that type by overload resolution on the arguments given.

Writing the assignment in the body instead,

```cpp
Binom(int n_, double p_) { n = n_; p = p_; }
```

means `n` and `p` are first default-initialized in phase one and then
overwritten in phase two -- two operations where one would do. For `int` and
`double` the difference is negligible and the compiler will optimize it away,
so here the argument is mainly one of habit. The reasons become real once the
members are not trivial: a `std::vector` member would be built empty and then
copy-assigned, and some members *cannot* be assigned at all. A `const` member,
a reference member, a member whose class has no default constructor, and the
arguments passed to a base class all have to appear in the initializer list, or
the code does not compile.

There is one more reason to prefer it here. If we assign in the body, there is
a window in which `n` and `p` hold indeterminate values: for built-in types,
default initialization of a member leaves the value undefined, and reading it
before the assignment is undefined behaviour. With the initializer list that
window does not exist.

## Exercise 1: Factorial

A recursive implementation. The base case `k <= 1` covers both $0! = 1$ and
$1! = 1$, and is what stops the recursion.

```cpp
inline int Binom::factorial(int k) const {

  if (k <= 1)
    return 1;

  return k * factorial(k - 1);

}
```

Test:

```cpp
Binom b(10, 0.5);
for (int i = 1; i <= 10; ++i)
    std::cout << b.factorial(i) << std::endl;
```

which prints `1 2 6 24 120 720 5040 40320 362880 3628800`, matching R:

```{r}
factorial(1:10)
```

### An iterative alternative

Nothing in the exercise requires recursion. A loop does the same job:

```cpp
inline int Binom::factorial(int k) const {

  int result = 1;
  for (int i = 2; i <= k; ++i)
    result *= i;

  return result;

}
```

The loop body never runs for `k <= 1`, so $0! = 1$ and $1! = 1$ come out
correctly without a separate base case.

Which one to prefer? The recursive version reads like the mathematical
definition $k! = k \times (k-1)!$, which is why it is the standard teaching
example, and it is the shorter of the two. The iterative version uses a single
stack frame, where the recursive one pushes a new frame for every call --
`factorial(10)` nests ten deep, and a large enough argument would overflow the
stack. Note that the recursion here is *not* tail recursive: the multiplication
`k * factorial(k - 1)` happens only after the inner call returns, so each frame
still has work pending and the compiler cannot mechanically rewrite it into a
loop. At `-O2` it will often inline and unroll the calls anyway, but that is an
optimisation we are relying on rather than a guarantee.

The general rule: recursion pays off when the problem is genuinely tree-shaped
-- traversing a tree, quicksort, divide and conquer -- where writing it
iteratively means managing an explicit stack by hand. Factorial is a straight
chain of one call each, so the loop loses nothing.

::: {.callout-warning}
## Integer overflow

The signature in the lab returns an `int`, which is 32 bits on most platforms
and therefore maxes out around $2.1 \times 10^9$. Since $13! = 6{,}227{,}020{,}800$,
`factorial(13)` silently overflows. For $n = 10$ we are safe, but a
production-quality version would return `double` (or `long double`) and, better
still, compute the log-factorial with `std::lgamma` — see the
[bonus section](#bonus-a-numerically-safe-dbinom-with-lgamma) at the end.
:::

## Exercise 2: Choose

$$
{a \choose b} = \frac{a!}{b!\,(a-b)!}
$$

The key detail is the cast: `factorial()` returns `int`, so dividing two of them
directly would perform *integer* division and truncate the result. Casting the
numerator (and denominator) to `double` first avoids that.

```cpp
inline double Binom::choose(int a, int b) const {

  if (b < 0 || b > a)
    return 0.0;

  return static_cast<double>(factorial(a)) /
    (static_cast<double>(factorial(b)) * static_cast<double>(factorial(a - b)));

}
```

The guard `b < 0 || b > a` reproduces R's behavior of returning 0 outside the
support, and also keeps us from calling `factorial()` with a negative argument
(which would recurse forever with a `k == 0` base case).

Test:

```cpp
Binom b(10, 0.5);
for (int i = 1; i <= 10; ++i)
    std::cout << b.choose(10, i) << std::endl;
```

gives `10 45 120 210 252 210 120 45 10 1`, matching R:

```{r}
choose(10, 1:10)
```

## Exercise 3: `dbinom`

Direct translation of

$$
\Pr\left(Y = k; n, p\right) = {n \choose k} p^k (1 - p)^{n - k}
$$

Here `n` and `p` are the *members* of the object, so we can refer to them
directly (writing `this->n` and `this->p` is equivalent and sometimes clearer).

```cpp
inline double Binom::dbinom(int k) const {

  if (k < 0 || k > n)
    return 0.0;

  return choose(n, k) * std::pow(p, k) * std::pow(1.0 - p, n - k);

}
```

Test:

```cpp
Binom b(10, 0.5);
for (int i = 0; i <= 10; ++i)
    std::cout << b.dbinom(i) << std::endl;
```

matching R:

```{r}
dbinom(0:10, 10, 0.5)
```

(`std::cout` prints 6 significant digits by default; use
`std::cout << std::setprecision(15)` from `<iomanip>` if you want to compare
more digits.)

## Exercise 4: Print

`std::printf` from `<cstdio>` takes the same format strings as R's `sprintf`,
so the format string can be copied over verbatim — we only need to append
`\n`, since `printf` does not add a newline.

```cpp
inline void Binom::print(int k) const {

  std::printf(
    "P(Y=%-2d; n=%d, p=%.2f) = %.4f\n",
    k, n, p, dbinom(k)
  );

}
```

`%-2d` left-aligns the integer in a field of width 2, which is what keeps the
`;` in the same column for `k = 0, ..., 9` and `k = 10`.

Running

```cpp
Binom b(10, 0.5);
for (int k = 0; k <= 10; ++k)
    b.print(k);
```

produces

```
P(Y=0 ; n=10, p=0.50) = 0.0010
P(Y=1 ; n=10, p=0.50) = 0.0098
P(Y=2 ; n=10, p=0.50) = 0.0439
P(Y=3 ; n=10, p=0.50) = 0.1172
P(Y=4 ; n=10, p=0.50) = 0.2051
P(Y=5 ; n=10, p=0.50) = 0.2461
P(Y=6 ; n=10, p=0.50) = 0.2051
P(Y=7 ; n=10, p=0.50) = 0.1172
P(Y=8 ; n=10, p=0.50) = 0.0439
P(Y=9 ; n=10, p=0.50) = 0.0098
P(Y=10; n=10, p=0.50) = 0.0010
```

which is identical to the R reference:

```{r}
sprintf(
  "P(Y=%-2d; n=%d, p=%.2f) = %.4f",
  0:10, 10, 0.5, dbinom(0:10, 10, 0.5)
  ) |>
  cat(sep = "\n")
```

## Aside: do we need `inline`?

`inline` is **not** needed in this program. Everything lives in a single
translation unit, so `int Binom::factorial(int k) const { ... }` would compile
and link exactly the same. The keyword earns its keep only when the
definitions sit in a header that is `#include`d by more than one `.cpp`:
without `inline` each inclusion emits the same symbol and the linker reports a
duplicate definition. (Member functions defined *inside* the class body — like
the constructor above — are implicitly `inline`, which is why they never need
it.) The lab asks for the `inline [return type] [class]::[function]` pattern
because that is the form you will use once you split the class into a `.hpp`,
as in `person.hpp` and `summary.hpp`, so we keep it here for consistency.

## Aside: what is `const` actually doing here?

All four member functions are declared `const`:

```cpp
int factorial(int k) const;
double choose(int a, int b) const;
double dbinom(int k) const;
void print(int k) const;
```

Strictly speaking, this program compiles and runs identically without them. So
why bother? Because `const` on a member function is a *promise*, checked by the
compiler, that calling it does not change the object. It buys you two things.

### 1. It stops you from modifying the object by accident

Inside a `const` member function, every data member is treated as read-only.
A typo like `n = k` — easy to write when you meant to compare, or when you were
reaching for a local variable — is caught immediately instead of silently
corrupting the object:

```cpp
inline int Binom::factorial(int k) const { n = k; return n; }
```

```
error: cannot assign to non-static data member within const member function 'factorial'
inline int Binom::factorial(int k) const { n = k; return n; }
                                           ~ ^
note: member function 'Binom::factorial' is declared const here
```

This is the payoff that matters while you are writing the class. `factorial`,
`choose`, `dbinom` and `print` are all *queries*: they read `n` and `p` and
compute an answer. Marking them `const` makes that design intent explicit and
gets it enforced. A setter such as `set_p(double)` would deliberately be left
non-`const`.

### 2. It lets callers use your object through a `const` handle

This is the reason `const` spreads through real codebases. Suppose someone
writes a helper that takes a `Binom` by constant reference — the standard way to
pass an object you do not intend to copy or modify:

```cpp
double expected_value(const Binom &b) {
  double out = 0.0;
  for (int k = 0; k <= 10; ++k)
    out += k * b.dbinom(k);   // only reads b
  return out;
}
```

If `dbinom` were *not* marked `const`, this would not compile — even though the
function plainly only reads:

```
error: 'this' argument to member function 'dbinom' has type 'const Binom',
       but function is not marked const
double total(const Binom &b) { return b.dbinom(0); }
                                      ^
```

The compiler cannot inspect the body to see that `dbinom` behaves itself; it
only trusts the signature. The same applies to a `const Binom b(10, 0.5);`
object, to a `Binom` member of some larger `const` object, and to storing
`Binom`s in a container you then iterate over with `const auto &`. Omitting
`const` does not just lose a safety check — it actively locks legitimate callers
out.

::: {.callout-tip}
## Rule of thumb

Mark a member function `const` unless it needs to modify the object. It costs
nothing at runtime (the compiler does not generate different code for the
arithmetic), and retrofitting it later is painful precisely because it is
contagious: one missing `const` deep in a call chain forces every caller above
it to drop `const` too.
:::

### A common error: `const` on the declaration but not the definition

The `const` is part of the function's signature, so it has to appear in **both**
places. Forget it on the out-of-line definition and the compiler does not see an
implementation of the function you declared — it sees an unrelated one:

```cpp
class Binom {
  // ...
  int factorial(int k) const;              // declared const
};

inline int Binom::factorial(int k) { ... } // definition forgot const
```

```
error: out-of-line definition of 'factorial' does not match any declaration in 'Binom'
note: member declaration does not match because it is const qualified
  int factorial(int k) const;
      ^                ~~~~~
```

The message points at the mismatch clearly enough once you have seen it once,
but "does not match any declaration" is confusing the first time — the fix is
always to compare the two signatures character by character, `const` included.

## Bonus: a numerically safe `dbinom` with `lgamma`

The implementation above is a faithful translation of the formula, but it is
fragile. It is worth understanding *why*, because the fix is a pattern you will
reuse constantly in statistical computing.

### Why the direct formula breaks

There are two separate failure modes, and they pull in opposite directions:

1. **The binomial coefficient overflows.** `factorial` returns an `int`, so it
   is already wrong at $13! = 6{,}227{,}020{,}800$:

   ```
   fact(13) as int = 1932053504   (true value 6227020800)
   ```

   Switching to `double` buys us room up to about $170!$, but no further.

2. **The powers underflow.** $p^k(1-p)^{n-k}$ shrinks geometrically. For
   $n = 1000$, $p = 0.5$ the factor is $2^{-1000} \approx 10^{-301}$, right at
   the edge of what a `double` can represent.

The insidious part is that these two problems nearly cancel: the true answer is
a perfectly ordinary number, we just cannot get there by computing a gigantic
quantity and multiplying it by a minuscule one. With `n = 20` the direct version
already returns a *negative probability*, and by `n = 1000` it gives up entirely:

```
n=20,   k=10:  direct = -1.522418863e-10   lgamma = 0.176197052
n=1000, k=500: direct = nan                lgamma = 0.02522501818
```

```{r}
# R's answers, for reference
dbinom(10, 20, 0.5)
dbinom(500, 1000, 0.5)
```

### The fix: work on the log scale

Take logs of the whole expression, so that products become sums and the huge and
tiny pieces cancel *additively* — in a range `double` handles comfortably — and
only exponentiate at the very end:

$$
\log\Pr(Y = k) = \log n! - \log k! - \log (n-k)! + k\log p + (n-k)\log(1-p)
$$

To get $\log k!$ without ever forming $k!$ we use the gamma function, which
interpolates the factorial:

$$
\Gamma(x) = \int_0^\infty t^{x-1}e^{-t}\,dt,
\qquad \Gamma(k + 1) = k! \ \text{ for integer } k \ge 0
$$

`std::lgamma(x)` from `<cmath>` returns $\log\Gamma(x)$ directly — it never
computes $\Gamma(x)$ itself, so nothing overflows. The shift by one is the part
people trip over: **`std::lgamma(k + 1.0)` is $\log k!$**, not
`std::lgamma(k)`.

```cpp
inline double Binom::dbinom(int k) const {

  if (k < 0 || k > n)
    return 0.0;

  // log(n!) - log(k!) - log((n-k)!)  ==  log(choose(n, k))
  double log_choose = std::lgamma(n + 1.0) -
    std::lgamma(k + 1.0) -
    std::lgamma(n - k + 1.0);

  // k*log(p) + (n-k)*log(1-p)
  double log_powers = k * std::log(p) + (n - k) * std::log1p(-p);

  return std::exp(log_choose + log_powers);

}
```

Three details worth naming:

- **`std::log1p(-p)` instead of `std::log(1.0 - p)`.** `log1p(x)` computes
  $\log(1 + x)$ accurately for small $|x|$. When $p$ is tiny, `1.0 - p` rounds
  to a nearby `double` and throws away the low-order bits of $p$ before the log
  ever sees them; `log1p(-p)` keeps them. Same reasoning as R's own `log1p`.
- **The `+ 1.0`, not `+ 1`.** Writing `std::lgamma(n + 1)` still works because
  the `int` promotes to `double`, but spelling out `1.0` makes the
  floating-point intent explicit and guards against surprises if `n` ever
  changes type.
- **Multiplying `k * std::log(p)` beats `std::pow(p, k)`.** It is both faster
  and keeps us on the log scale, where there is nothing to underflow.

For $n = 10$ this returns exactly the same values as the direct version:

```
0.0009765625  0.0097656250  0.0439453125  0.1171875000  0.2050781250
0.2460937500  0.2050781250  0.1171875000  0.0439453125  0.0097656250
0.0009765625
```

but it keeps working for $n$ in the millions.

### Going one step further

If you only ever need the log-density — which is the common case, since
likelihoods are summed on the log scale — stop before the `std::exp` and return
`log_choose + log_powers`. That is what R's `dbinom(..., log = TRUE)` gives you,
and it avoids throwing away precision (and possibly underflowing to 0) on the
very last step:

```{r}
dbinom(500, 1000, 0.5, log = TRUE)
```

Exponentiating a sum of logs is accurate to within a rounding error or two,
which is the best any implementation can do. R's actual `dbinom` goes further
still and uses a saddle-point expansion (Loader's algorithm) for large $n$, so
the last digit may differ from the `lgamma` version — both are correct to
roughly full `double` precision.
